title: UPDATE: OpenAI Math Papers Destroyed Careers, NYU Professor Says
summary:
NYU math professor Tristan Buckmaster said he had heard of three people whose entire research programs were “obliterated” by OpenAI’s Oct. 6 release of 722 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts. “This recent dump of papers on Tuesday destroyed the careers of early career mathematicians. We had whole research programs wiped out,” he said. The Verge interviewed more than three dozen mathematicians, with others reporting that grant proposals had been wiped out and some results could have put human researchers in contention for a Fields Medal.

Buckmaster also accused OpenAI of a conflict of interest, alleging that research proposals summarized by panelists using AI end up in its training data. “They have all the mathematicians and scientists' research programs in their training data and how they're going to go about it,” he said. The release contains 372 families of related results from an unreleased internal model, rather than solutions to 722 separate open problems. OpenAI has withdrawn three manuscripts and revised 14 others.

Other researchers are building on the work. Rohan Arun published four improvements covering van der Waerden, Sidorenko, unit distances and matrix multiplication, including a conditional 500-fold increase in an exponent coefficient for the van der Waerden result. Separately, contributor SJ Swapnil Jain raised the exponent saving parameter in OpenAI’s theoretical integer multiplication bound to 6.6857 × 10⁻⁴ from the original 2⁻¹⁸². The increase concerns a parameter, not practical multiplication speed. Jain wrote, “We seem to be approaching a wall. Gains now come in fractions of a percent.”

Eleventh update to OpenAI problem #109 (integer multiplication): κ rises to 2⁻¹⁰·⁵⁴⁷, still past 2⁻¹¹.

Witness value: κ = 2⁻¹⁰·⁵⁴⁷ = 6.6857 × 10⁻⁴ 
(tightened from κ = 2⁻¹⁸²)

This κ is about 1.09 fold our previous witness value κ = 2⁻¹⁰·⁶⁶⁶ = 6.1534 × 10⁻⁴, and a 2¹⁷¹ fold improvement in κ over the original OAI result.

We seem to be approaching a wall. Gains now come in fractions of a percent. The next real jump needs a big breakthrough which we are unable to find yet.

selectedTweets.text:
Fields Medalists Are Wrong: Why AI Is an Accelerant, Not a Bane, to Progress in Mathematics

On the heels of OpenAI having solved the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, about half of the living Fields Medalists signed an open letter titled “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics”. 

As of October 4th, 2026, the letter was ultimately signed by over 8,000 (and counting) mathematicians and academics in related fields.

Conjecture Institute Fellow and mathematician @PaulRRobichaud  and President @ChipkinLogan disagree with the spirit of the letter, which is essentially that AI is a problem for mathematics. 

On the contrary, it is a catalyst that opens entirely new vistas to mathematicians that were heretofore unreachable.
